abstract.p: Crimean–Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV) is a tick-borne pathogen causes hemorrhagic disease with high fatality rates, and no approved vaccines/antivirals currently exist. The viral L protein contains a unique ovarian tumor (OTU) protease domain that cleaves ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like modifiers from host proteins, thereby aiding immune evasion and viral replication. Targeting the OTU domain represents a promising strategy for therapeutic intervention. Peptides obtained from Moringa oleifera proteome that mimic the binding mode of the endogenous ubiquitin molecule. These peptides were computationally screened for their ability to bind the OTU protease domain, incorporating both conventional cysteine protease inhibitors and protein–protein interaction interface mimetics. This study revealed Pep31 with a strong balance of binding affinity, solubility, and structural stability, highlighting its potential as a novel OTU protease inhibitor. While our findings are computational, they provide a foundation for experimental validation and the future development of peptide-based antivirals targeting CCHFV.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Crimean Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV) is an imperative zoonotic pathogen causing severe viral hemorrhagic fever outbreaks with a high mortality rate. CCHF is an infection primarily transmitted to humans through the bite of infected ticks of the genus Hyalomma1, while CCHFV belongs to the genus Orthonairovirus, in the family Nairoviridae, within the order of Bunyavirales2. Cases of CCHF virus infection have been reported in the literature in more than fifty countries in Africa, Europe, and Asia. It causes sporadic outbreaks of hemorrhagic fever with mild or severe symptoms such as muscle pain affecting the neck, back, and head, sore eyes, and photophobia, which may rapidly develop into sever hemorrhagic manifestations 3–5. Recent reports suggest that deaths from CCHFV are increasing in endemic areas because of ticks carrying the virus6,7. Climate change, a rise in tick numbers, increased human exposure to animals, and the improvement of assays to detect viral infection are the main causes of the elevated prevalence of the infection in various populations worldwide. Currently, no approved drug or vaccine is available for the treatment or prevention of CCHF. Therefore, developing effective therapeutic agents remains a critical global health priority to combat CCHF virus infection8. The RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) of CCHF virus, particularly its OTU protease domain, plays a pivotal role in the CCHFV life cycle and pathogenesis by processing viral polyproteins for the replication of the viral genome9, making it an attractive target for antiviral drug development. The large (L) segment of the CCHFV genome encodes the viral deubiquitinase (vDUB) domain10. These vDUBs are explicitly involved in the evasion of host immune responses by targeting UB and ISG15, both of which are key regulators of innate immunity11. These virally encoded DUBs reverse ubiquitination, thus altering host signaling pathways, which are critical for the induction of various antiviral and cellular pro-inflammatory innate immune responses12. In addition to removing ubiquitin from host proteins, several viral DUBs (vDUBs) also eliminate ISG15, further inhibiting antiviral responses10. It is noteworthy that the CCHF virus DUB is also critical for viral replication13. The OTU protease domain within CCHFV RdRp is an excellent target for antiviral drugs because of its combined replicative and/or deubiquitinating properties, which directly contribute to pathogenesis during viral infection in vivo, making it an attractive antiviral drug target. Finding bigger, hydrophobic compounds that also cover the ubiquitin-binding sites seems distinctive, as therapeutically active-site inhibitors of OTUs are not selective14. Our research was aimed at identifying novel antiviral peptides with significant inhibitory activity against the OTU protease domain of RdRp from the CCHFV. Utilizing the whole proteome of Moringa oleifera, a plant known for its diverse bioactive compounds, we sought to discover peptides with potential antiviral properties through a comprehensive in silico approach. The entire proteome of Moringa oleifera was subjected to in silico digestion to generate a library of peptides. These peptides were then screened for antimicrobial and antiviral properties. Soluble peptides were further evaluated for their physicochemical properties, hemolytic activity, and antigenicity. Selected peptides demonstrating favorable profiles underwent antiviral activity assessment. The most promising antiviral peptides were docked against the OTU protease, with their effectiveness evaluated based on significant docked rank score and MM-GBSA ranked score. Three peptides, named Pep23, Pep31, and Pep42, were shortlisted and analyzed for their binding patterns with the OTU protease compared to the binding pattern of a modified ubiquitin variant known to inhibit OTU protease (PDB ID: 5V5H). These peptides complexed with the OTU domain were also subjected to MD simulations to evaluate binding patterns, and potential inhibitory mechanisms. The identified antiviral peptides demonstrated strong binding affinity and inhibitory potential against the OTU protease domain. The comparative analysis with a known inhibitor also provided insights into the binding efficiency and potential mechanism of action of these peptides. MD simulations further supported their stability and interaction dynamics within the viral protease, highlighting their potential as promising candidates for further experimental validation. The discovery of these antiviral peptides represents a significant step forward in the search for effective therapeutics against CCHFV. Through the bioactive potential of Moringa oleifera’s proteome and advanced in silico screening, we identified peptide candidates with promise for further investigation. These findings highlight the importance of innovative approaches in antiviral drug discovery and offer a novel pathway for developing effective treatments against diseases caused by highly pathogenic viruses like the CCHF virus.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p:
In the presented study, a bioinformatics-based structural biology approach is used to search for OTU protease inhibitors, whereas MD simulation analysis was performed to explore the binding pattern of obtained peptides interacting with the OTU protease binding site. The aim of this study is to find contact inhibitors of OTU protease; the schematic workflow of this study is given in Fig. 1.Fig. 1
Complete workflow of study, to discover peptides from Moringa oleifera serving as contact inhibitor of OTU protease of CCHFV.

sec.title: Genomic and proteomic data mining
sec.p: The whole proteome of Moringa oleifera was downloaded from Online Resource for Community Annotation of Eukaryotes (ORCAE) database (https://bioinformatics.psb.ugent.be/gdb/aocc/morolbgi/Moringa_version2/15. Chang et. al. sequenced the Moringa oleifera genome into 14 pseudochromosomes with a total length of 236.4 Mb. Using a combination of protein homology, ab initio prediction, and RNA-seq-based evidence, a total of 22,714 protein-coding genes were identified in the sequenced genome of Moringa oleifera, of which 93.1% were supported by transcriptome data.

sec.title: In-silico digestion of proteome
sec.p: The complete proteome of Moringa oleifera was subjected to in silico digestion to generate nested peptides. RapidPeptidesGenerator (RPG v2.0.3), a Python3-based library for simulating enzymatic hydrolysis using various peptidases16, was employed. For concurrent digestion, the enzymes pepsin, trypsin, proline-endopeptidase, and chymotrypsin were used to simulate cleavage of entire Moringa oleifera proteome.

sec.title: Shortlisting of potential peptides-peptides solubility filtering
sec.p: Initially, the peptides obtained from in silico digestion were assessed and filtered based on a set of predefined rules. Peptides were discarded if the first or last amino acid is charged, if the number of glycine or proline residues exceeded one, if any single amino acid constituted more than 25% of the total sequence, or if the proportion of charged and/or hydrophobic amino acids exceeded 45% of the sequence. Additionally, peptides containing fewer than 20 amino acid residues were excluded. Furthermore, the solubility of the remaining peptides was predicted using SoluProt v1.017, a standalone Python 3-based tool trained on a curated dataset of experimentally validated soluble peptides expressed in Escherichia coli.

sec.title: Prediction of antiviral activity and physicochemical property analysis of peptides
sec.p: The activity of plant-based soluble peptides was predicted by PTPAMP (Prediction Tool for Plant-derived Antimicrobial Peptides) (http://14.139.61.8/PTPAMP/ss.php)18, which predicts various peptides activities including antimicrobial, antifungal, and antiviral properties. The soluble peptides which demonstrated antiviral properties, were evaluated for their activity as either toxin or non-toxin and allergen or non-allergen using online server of ToxinPred v3.0 (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/toxinpred3/index.html)19 and AllerTOP v2.0 (https://www.ddg-pharmfac.net/AllerTOP/)20. Furthermore, the non-toxin and non-allergen peptides were subjected to their hemolytic activity evaluation using the online server HAPPENN (https://research.timmons.eu/happenn)21.

sec.title: Modelling of 3D peptide structure
sec.p: Modelling of peptides including non-toxic and non-allergen like and non-hemolytic proposed viral peptides was carried out using Pepfold and ITessor. The structure of these peptides showing significant docked rank score and MM-GBSA ranked score, were further verified by Verify 3D. PROCHECK was then used to obtain Ramachandran plot to evaluate the structural accuracy of the modelled peptides.

sec.title: Target enzyme retrieval and protein-peptide docking
sec.p: The OTU crystal structure was fetched from the PDB database using accession ID:5V5H that was resolved at a resolution of 1.5 Å using X-ray crystallography11. Along with OTU domain, the crystal structure comprised of Ubiquitin variant CC.2 and 4-(2-Hydrooxyethyl)-1-Piprazine Ethanesulfonic Acid (EPE), Zn+2, and Na+. During receptor preparation, only chain A (OTU domain), Zn+2, and Na+ were retained while chain B and EPE were removed. The three peptides were subjected to blind docking using HawkDock server (http://cadd.zju.edu.cn/hawkdock/) ten binding poses of each peptide were obtained based on more negative binding energy. In addition, molecular mechanics-generalized born solvent accessible surface area (MM/GBSA) was calculated for the best docked peptide molecule to the OTU peptidase domain by MM/GBSA program of HawkDock server.

sec.title: Molecular dynamics simulations-OTU domain complexed with UbV/Peptides
sec.p: The simulation systems comprising the OTU protease complexed with UbV and peptides, were prepared using the xLEaP module of AmberTools2322. The systems were modeled with the AMBER FF19SB force field23. Each simulation system was neutralized using six Na+ ions as counter-ions that was followed by solvation with the TIP3P water model under periodic boundary conditions at a distance of 8 Å. The initial configuration of the systems was subjected to energy minimization using the L-BFGS optimization algorithm24 until convergence to remove bad intra- and inter molecular interactions. Following minimization, the system was equilibrated for 2 picoseconds (1000 steps) under NPT conditions to achieve a stable structure and then subjected to production MD simulation. To converge the energy, a tolerance of 10 kJ/mol was used. During equilibration and production MD simulations, temperature and pressure were fixed at 300 K and 1 atm, respectively. To maintain the temperature and pressure, Langevin thermostat and Monte Carlo barostat method with an integration time step of 2 fs were used. SHAKE algorithm was applied to constrain all bonds involving hydrogen atoms25 with a cutoff distance of 12 Å. Particle Mesh Ewald algorithm26, was utilized for non-bonded interactions. By adjusting the keyword “removeCMMotion” to True and setting “rigidwater” to False, we have maintained the center of periodicity and allowed water molecules to become flexible during simulation time. The other parameters for simulations include the “EwaldErrorTolerance” of 0.001 and the “friction” of 1.0/picosecond. For each system, MD simulations of 500 ns with a total cumulative time of 2 µs were performed in OpenMM27.

sec.title: Analysis of the simulation trajectories
sec.p: The preliminary analysis was based on the sequence alignment of the peptides with UbV to assess the structural and functional similarities. The alignment of the sequences was performed using MAFFT, a multiple sequence alignment tool28. The simulation trajectories were analyzed for the stability check of the simulation via RMSD, and averaged RMSF was performed for of each amino acid residue using MDAnalysis 2.8.029. The representative structures obtained from the simulation trajectories were visualized by PyMOL program30. DSSP module of CPPTRAJ31 was used to monitor the changes in the secondary structure elements of OTU protease bound to the peptides and UbV. Interactions between the target protein and peptides were evaluated in comparison to OTU-UbV complex with the help of GetContacts tool (https://getcontacts.github.io/). The interaction analysis included H-bond (including backbone to backbone, side-chain to backbone, and side-chain to side-chain), vdW, salt-bridge, and π-cation interactions.

sec.title: Principal component analysis and free energy landscape
sec.p: The collective conformational changes, induced by UbV and peptides (Pep23, Pep31, Pep42), were studied using principal component analysis (PCA) on last 250 ns simulation data32. Initially, the rotational and translational motions were eliminated and the coordinates were superimposed onto a reference structure, and then the positional covariance matrix and eigenvectors of the coordinates were calculated. The eigenvectors and eigenvalues were generated by “gmx covar”. Then the congenerous eigenvectors were analyzed by the “gmx analog” tool of GROMACS33. The eigenvalues were calculated by diagonalizing the covariance matrix of the protein fluctuations. After performing essential component analysis, the stable conformations were extracted from the Gibbs free energy plot.

Results
sec.p:
The whole proteome of Moringa oleifera comprised of over 22,000 proteins. The length distribution of these proteins is given in Fig. 1. Most proteins have sequences longer than 1000 amino acids; only 4.74% of proteins (1044 sequences) consist of fewer than 100 amino acids. The whole proteome of Moringa oleifera was analyzed using BLASTP v2.13 to see if it contained nested hemolytic peptides. We found only a single hemolytic peptide (sequence “ANRLLEAYKMLLKFLGNLR”36) as a nested peptide in the whole proteome. Since there is a possibility of nested peptides that possess anti-viral activity and can only be expressed after the cleavage done by various digestive enzymes37, considering that Moringa oleifera is consumed as a health-care food and medicine, pepsin, trypsin, and chymotrypsin from the RPG v2.0.3 tool were selected as model enzymes to concurrently hydrolyze the whole set of proteins. This concurrent hydrolysis of given proteins resulted in the generation of more than 3.7 million peptides of various lengths. The initial filtration of peptides done based on the rules defined in the methodology section resulted in the shortlisting of peptides from 3.7 million to only 8321 peptides given in sup-file2.fa. These 8321 peptides were subjected for their solubility prediction and only forty-three peptides were shortlisted based on their solubility, predicted by SoluProt v1.0. These soluble peptides are given in Table 1 with their physicochemical properties. These soluble peptides have amino acid in the range of 20–33 residues. These peptides were subjected for their toxicity and allergenicity prediction, results given in Table 2. Only Pep29 was predicted as a toxin, whereas the remaining forty-two peptides were predicted as non-toxic. Out of forty-three soluble peptides only twenty-four peptides (Pep01, 06, 07, 09, 10, 11, 13, 15, 16, 17, 21, 23, 25, 26, 27, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 36, 38, 39, and 42) were predicted as non-allergen (Table 2). These twenty-four soluble, non-toxin, non-allergic peptides were predicted for their antimicrobial activity by the online server of PTPAMP. The specificity of this server is to predict the various antimicrobial activities of plant-based peptides, as the Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithm of PTPAMP is trained on plant-based peptides that were collected from PlantPepDB, while Amino Acid Composition (AAC) and Dipeptide Composition (DPC) are used to define peptide features for SVM model training. sec.title: Docking studies
sec.p: A total of thirteen predicted antiviral peptides were subjected to docking studies. The peptide structures were modelled using PEP-FOLD 4.0. The peptides were blindly docked onto the OTU protease domain of the RdRP of CCHFV, allowing binding to any energetically favorable region. The binding energies of the docked peptides, along with their MMGBSA ranked scores, are provided in Table 4. Based on significant docking and MMGBSA ranked scores, three peptides (Pep23, Pep31, and Pep42) were shortlisted for MD simulation studies.

Molecular interactions mediated by these shortlisted peptides were analyzed and compared with the binding interactions mediated by the modified ubiquitin molecule present as a co-crystallized inhibitor of OTU protease in the X-ray crystal structure (PDB ID: 5V5H). Similar patterns of molecular interactions were observed between the antiviral peptides (see S1, S2, and S3 Table for detailed interaction mediated by Pep23, Pep31, and Pep42, respectively) and the viral deubiquitinase/OTU protease as observed in the interaction analysis of the X-ray crystalized enzyme with the ubiquitin variant (PDB ID: 5V5H); detailed interactions are given in S4 Table. Common amino acids found interacting with the inhibiting antiviral peptides and ubiquitin variant (UbV) are Glu(78 and 98), Arg92, Trp99, Gly100, Ser101, Thr102, Ile(118 and 131), His146, Gln149, and Phe152, shown in Fig. 3. Analysis of the CCHF virus deubiquitinase/OTU protease-UbV complex revealed that UbV mediated ten H-bonds with Gln16, Asn20, Pro77, Glu78, Arg80, Gly100, Ser101, and Thr102 of the OTU protease. UbV also formed two salt bridges with OE1 and OE2 of Glu78 as well. Detailed H-bonds and salt bridges with bond length are given in Table 6. Pep23 mediated four H-bonds and one salt bridge with CCHF virus deubiquitinase/OTU protease (Fig. 4). As given in Table 6, each OG of Ser14 and OG Ser17 (Pep23) mediated two H-bonds with O of Trp99, OE2 of Glu104, NH1 of Arg92, and OE1 of Glu98 (OTU protease) with a bond distance of 3.3, 2.97, 2.39, and 2.97 Å, respectively. A salt bridge was formed by NE2 of His7 of Pep23 with OE1 of Glu78 of OTU protease. Pep31 mediated hydrophobic/non-bonded interactions with the OTU protease binding site. sec.title: Structural and dynamical properties of OTU protease
sec.p:
The binding partners of the OTU protease consisted of 78, 21, 29, and 28 amino acid residues for UbV, Pep23, Pep31, and Pep42, respectively. The simulation systems based on the peptides complexed with OTU protease were analyzed in detail. Initially, the system’s stability of each complex was assessed by computing RMSD of OTU’s backbone atoms. The RMSD for all systems fluctuated between 1.5 and 2.7 Å, as depicted in Fig. 5a, demonstrating overall system stability, which helped to extract the trajectories based on the final 250 ns of the simulation for the evaluation of other properties. The dynamic flexibility of the protein in each system was identified by performing RMSF analysis, (Fig. 5b). Peptides, Pep23 and Pep42, when bound to OTU protease, demonstrated enhanced flexibility at both catalytic sites of the protease. In the case of OTU protease bound with Pep23, the flexibility of catalytic site 1 increased from 0.8 Å to 2.4 as shown in Fig. 5b.Fig. 5
System stability of peptide-bound OTU protease. (a) Root mean square deviation, (b) Average flexibility of each amino acid residue of OTU protease, (c) 3D-representation depicting the flexibility of OTU protease. Change in secondary structure, DSSP profile of (d) OTU protease (residue ranges from 1–164), and e) binders (residues range from 165 onward) throughout simulation time.

The variation in the protein secondary structure elements was evaluated in terms of DSSP analysis for all complexes including the evaluation of structural variation of UbV and peptides. During simulation, UbV maintained its secondary structure while being bound to OTU protease; however, significant structural variations were observed for the peptides (Fig. 4e and 5d). In the case of OTU protease-Pep23 and OTU protease-Pep42 complexes, the secondary structure elements in OTU protease were also perturbed since Pep23 perturbed the secondary structure of the protein’s catalytic site. The region spanning residues 27 to 60 and 74 to 91 (catalytic site 2 of OTU protease) exhibited significant disruption in the secondary structure throughout the simulation period. No drastic changes were observed in the secondary structure of the protein when bound to UbV or Pep31; however, Pep31 underwent structural variation in particular residues ranging from 164 to 174 (Fig. 5e). These residues exhibited continuous structural variations during the simulation, frequently switching between 3₁₀-helix and turn conformations. This indicated an inability to maintain a stable secondary structure and reflected localized instability. In addition, residues from position 180 onwards lost their secondary structure. Nevertheless, larger structural variations were observed in Pep23 and Pep42 compared to Pep31.

sec.title: Inter-molecular interaction based on physicochemical similarities
sec.p:
Prior to the evaluation of other dynamical properties, sequence alignment of the peptides with UbV was performed to assess the physicochemical similarities of all the peptides bound to OTU protease. As shown in Fig. 6a, the sequence alignment revealed an overall low sequence identity of the peptides with UbV, largely due to differences in sequence length. Based on the alignment, the predicted biochemical properties, displayed in Fig. 6c, showed a higher fraction of hydrophobic residues in Pep31. Moreover, Pep31 exhibited a higher degree of similarity to UbV in both hydrophobic residue composition and cysteine content. In contrast to other peptides, the residues of Pep31 were also predicted to facilitate stronger interactions through hydrophobic and van der Waals (vdW) forces38. On the other hand, Pep23 and Pep42 contained highly polar and disorder-promoting residues such as glutamine (Q), serine (S), and threonine (T), which tend to prevent the formation of stable secondary structures.Fig. 6
(a) Sequence alignment, and (b) 3-D representative of UbV and all three peptides, color based Taylor. (c) Bar plot depicted biochemical properties based on amino acid composition.

The intermolecular interactions between the protein and the peptides, including UbV were examined in terms of electrostatic (H-bond, salt-bridge, and π -cation) and non-electrostatic (vdW) interactions. Flare plots of these interactions are shown in Fig. 7, where the line width indicates the interaction strength and the bold and thick line represent consistent interactions throughout the simulation. Based on these plots, it was found that OTU protease-UbV and OTU protease-Pep23 exhibited high fractions of H-bonds. In contrast, fewer residues contributed to the electrostatic interaction in the OTU protease-Pep31 complex, likely due to its higher hydrophobic residue content (Fig. 6c). In addition, Pep31 exhibited a large number of residues involved in vdW interactions with OTU protease compared to Pep23 and Pep42 peptides. These interaction patterns were well-aligned with those observed in the docking results, and the UbV interaction patterns with the protein also matched prior experimental data39. Other interactions reported for UbV with OTU protease included, residue-residue interactions such as H-bond (A.Q149-B.W241), vdW (A.I131-B.L173, A.I131-B.L235), and π-cation (A.R92-B.W241), which were also consistent with our study39 (Fig. 7). The OTU protease has been reported to have two catalytic sites, which comprise residues D37, G38, N39, C40, K71, and H151 for catalytic site-1, and Y89 to W99 for catalytic site-2 (Kocabaş and Ergin 2016). In the catalytic site-1, the residues C40 and H151 were the key residues that actively participate in the catalytic activity40, whereas other critical residues include Q16 and A12940. Across all peptide-bound OTU proteases, both residues (Q16 and A129) showed strong vdW interactions. However, the H-bond interactions of Q16 were absent in the OTU protease-Pep31 complex, but were in the rest of the peptide-protein complexes. Moreover, the crucial residue (C40) of the OTU protease40, depicted strong vdW interactions with the residues (S185 and C186) of Pep31 as shown in Fig. 7b. The other residue of Pep31, phenylalanine (F189) formed π-cation interactions with R33 and H151, as depicted in Fig. 7c. In case of Pep23 and Pep42, more residues were involved in forming H-bonds, but with fewer occupancy values, resulting in a less favorable energy contribution from electrostatic interaction.Fig. 7
Protein–Protein interactions, (a) Flare plot and 3D-representation of H-bond interactions, (b) flare plot for vdW interaction, and (c) π-cation and salt-bridge for all the complexes.

Protein–protein interactions (PPIs) mainly involve multiple weak, non-covalent interactions, including electrostatic interactions (Eelec), hydrogen bonds, vdW interactions, and hydrophobic effects. It is therefore not straightforward to accurately estimate the binding affinity of PPIs. However, the energy contributions of different types of interactions stabilizing the binding of the peptides, including UbV, to the OTU protease were evaluated using MM-PB/GBSA analysis performed on the last 10,000 snapshots taken from the simulation trajectories. This analysis is considered a powerful approach for exploring potential PPIs in terms of energy and has significant applications in drug design. All calculated binding energies are summarized in Table 7. MM-GBSA and MM-PBSA results revealed that UbV exhibited the most favorable binding energy (-71.94 in GB and -72.26 kcal/mol in PB), primarily driven by strong electrostatic (-366 kcal/mol) and van der Waals (-109 kcal/mol) interactions in both MM-GBSA and MM-PBSA analysis, despite significant desolvation penalties (418 and 414 kcal/mol). This behavior was attributed to the presence of charged and hydrophobic residues, as illustrated in Fig. 6b and c. In contrast, peptides, Pep23, Pep31, and Pep42 showed less favorable binding energies: -50.23, -57.09, -32.88 kcal/mol (GB) and -41.78, -52.54, -40.08 kcal/mol (PB), respectively. Among these peptides, Pep31 exhibited the most promising energy profile with balanced electrostatic (-85.87 kcal/mol) and van der Waals (-60.15 kcal/mol) contributions, with a moderate solvation penalty (Table 7), attributed to hydrophobic (A, P, V) and cysteine residues. Pep23 and Pep42 exhibited unfavorable electrostatics (141.32 and 190.1 kcal/mol in GB and PB, respectively); however, they showed favorable solvation energies in both GB (-122.29, and -159.41 kcal/mol) and PB (-113.84, and -166.61 kcal/mol) calculations, indicating that these peptides were more stable in the solvated (unbound) state than in the binding site. This weak binding is attributed to the presence of polar/disordered residues (Q, S, and T). The UbV and Pep31 also showed strong gas-phase energies, with respective GGAS values of -475.11 and -146.02 kcal/mol, mainly due to electrostatics, while solvation effects (GSOLV) significantly influenced overall binding. sec.title: Principal component and free energy landscape analyses of OTU protease complexes
sec.p:
PCA is a powerful tool for analyzing collective motion conformational dynamics induced by mutation and ligand binding41. To identified the collective motions and conformational landscapes associated UbV and peptide binding, PCA was performed on the Cα atoms of OTU protease. The resulting states were further analyzed using free energy landscape (FEL) calculations to characterize the distribution of conformational states. The initial twenty eigenvectors shown in Fig. 9a, demonstrated the overall OTU protease dynamics. The two initial eigenvectors were selected for further analysis and their phase space shown in Fig. 9b. Among the complexes, the OTU protease-UbV exhibited the highest eigenvalue for PC1, signifying pronounced collective motion along a dominant direction. In contrast, the OTU protease-Pep31 complex displayed comparatively lower eigenvalues, reflecting reduced large scale fluctuations and more constrained dynamics. On projecting the trajectories onto the PC1 and PC2 subspace explored dissimilar conformational sampling pattern among the systems. The OTU protease-UbV, and OTU protease-Pep31 occupied a rigid and well-defined region, identified stable conformational ensembles. In contrast, the OTU protease-Pep23 and OTU protease–Pep42 systems exhibited broader distributions along both PCs (PC1 and PC2), demonstrating greater conformational flexibility. Furthermore, the RMSF on each residue were analyzed along initial two PCs (Fig. 9c). The OTU protease-Pep23 and OTU protease-Pep42 complex displayed pronounced fluctuations across several residue regions, demonstrating increased local flexibility and structural rearrangements. In contrast, both OTU protease-UbV and OTU protease-Pep31 exhibited comparatively reduced fluctuations. The OTU protease bound with UbV and Pep31 have similar mobility pattern as depicted in Fig. 9d, and f. Notably, the OTU protease-Pep42 complex displayed multiple distinct minima on the FEL, indicating the presence of two energetically separated conformational sub-states. sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The active site of viral OTU proteases (vOTUs) is structurally well-defined, enabling rational design of small-molecule inhibitors that occupy the catalytic pocket with high affinity. However, due to the high degree of conservation of the catalytic triad among human, bacterial, and viral proteases, achieving selectivity through active-site targeting remains challenging. To ensure viral target specificity, it is essential to consider additional ubiquitin-binding hotspots that are unique to the viral protein. These regions may be selectively blocked or conformationally modulated to disrupt ubiquitin recognition14. Therefore, drug discovery strategies should prioritize compounds that integrate characteristics of both classical cysteine protease inhibitors and protein–protein interaction (PPI) inhibitors, offering a dual mechanism to enhance selectivity and efficacy.

sec.title: Peptide screening and safety filtering
sec.p: To expedite the process of drug discovery and explore the potential of protein- and peptide-based strategies, we used peptides obtained from in silico digestion of the Moringa oleifera proteome to target the CCHF viral OTU protease. This protease plays a key role in evading the host’s innate immune response by suppressing interferon signaling and promoting viral replication. The dataset analyzed comprised over 22,000 protein sequences15, with most proteins exceeding 1000 amino acids in length, shown in Fig. 1. This size distribution suggests a proteome dominated by large, multifunctional proteins, typical of plant species with complex secondary metabolism and defense mechanisms. The identification of antiviral peptides—Pep23, Pep31, and Pep42—exhibiting significant binding affinities and specific interactions with the OTU protease domain of the CCHFV RdRp represents a notable advancement in antiviral research. This is particularly significant in the context of emerging zoonotic pathogens such as CCHFV, which pose ongoing threats to global public health. The study highlights the therapeutic potential harbored within the Moringa oleifera proteome and underscores the utility of comprehensive in silico methodologies as effective tools in the early stages of antiviral drug discovery. A primary screening using BLASTP detected only a single known hemolytic peptide sequence (ANRLLEAYKMLLKFLGNLR,36). This very low incidence (~ 0.0045% of the proteome) highlights the relative safety of Moringa oleifera proteins with respect to intrinsic hemolytic potential in their intact form. This finding aligns with the traditional dietary use of Moringa, supporting its reputation as a safe nutritional and medicinal plant. Recognizing that bioactive peptides can be latent within larger proteins and released upon proteolytic processing37, the entire proteome was subjected to simulated hydrolysis by pepsin, trypsin, and chymotrypsin. The concurrent digestion yielded more than 3.7 million peptide fragments of diverse lengths and sequences, reflecting the vast theoretical diversity of the Moringa peptidome. From this vast pool, peptides were initially filtered using defined parameters in the study’s methodology, yielding 8,321 peptides suitable for further evaluation. Solubility prediction with SoluProt v1.0 narrowed this to only 43 peptides, indicating that the majority of proteolytic fragments are likely insoluble under physiological conditions-a key factor limiting their bioavailability and therapeutic potential. These 43 peptides ranged between 20 and 33 amino acids, a size suitable for therapeutic applications—large enough to exhibit biological activity but small enough to avoid rapid degradation or clearance. Toxicity and allergenicity predictions revealed that only one peptide (Pep29) was classified as toxic (Table 2), while the remaining peptides were non-toxic. Additionally, 24 peptides were predicted as non-allergenic, a crucial factor in considering potential therapeutic or nutraceutical use. The removal of allergenic and toxic sequences enhances safety, reducing the risk of adverse immunological reactions upon parenteral administration. Out of the non-toxic, non-allergenic peptides, thirteen were predicted as antiviral peptides (AVPs) by the PTPAMP server. PTPAMP’s training on plant-derived peptides adds reliability to these predictions, as it accommodates unique features of plant peptides not always captured by general AMP/AVP prediction tools. The prediction of AVPs from Moringa aligns with previous reports suggesting the plant’s broad antimicrobial and antiviral activities, contributing to its ethnopharmacological reputation. To investigate potential peptide-virus interactions, the structures of the thirteen predicted AVPs were modeled. PEP-FOLD 4.0 demonstrated higher accuracy in modeling a benchmark peptide (AMN) compared to I-TASSER, as evidenced by similarity in secondary structure features (β-sheets and turns). Therefore, PEP-FOLD 4.0 was chosen for modeling the candidate AVPs. Ramachandran plots were used to validate the structural integrity of key peptide models (Pep23, Pep31, and Pep42). All residues in these peptides were located within either the most favored or additionally allowed regions, with only minimal residues falling into generously allowed zones. This suggests that the peptides are likely to adopt stable conformations in solution, crucial for maintaining biological activity and binding specificity.

sec.title: Docking and interaction analysis
sec.p: Docking was performed using peptide structures modeled by PEP-FOLD 4.0, allowing binding across any energetically favorable region of the target protein. Based on docking rank and MMGBSA scores (Table 5), Pep23, Pep31, and Pep42 were shortlisted for further MD simulations. Comparative interaction analyses revealed that these peptides engage the OTU protease at sites overlapping with those involved in binding the co-crystallized modified UbV inhibitor in the crystal structure of the enzyme (PDB ID: 5V5H). Several conserved residues—including Glu78, Glu98, Arg92, Trp99, Gly100, Ser101, Thr102, Ile118, Ile131, His146, Gln149, and Phe152—were identified as common interaction partners for both UbV and the antiviral peptides (Fig. 3, Fig. 6, Table 6). Detailed examination of the OTU–UbV complex showed UbV mediates ten hydrogen bonds and two salt bridges, notably involving Glu78 and other active-site residues critical for substrate recognition (Table 6). Similarly, Pep23 formed four hydrogen bonds and one salt bridge with the OTU protease. Specifically, Ser14 and Ser17 in Pep23 formed hydrogen bonds with Trp99, Glu104, Arg92, and Glu98, with bond lengths of 2.39—3.30 Å. A salt bridge was observed between His7 of Pep23 and Glu78 of the protease, suggesting potential competitive inhibition of the viral deubiquitinase activity. In contrast, Pep31 displayed predominantly hydrophobic interactions, with only a single hydrogen bond detected between Ala7 of Pep31 and Thr102 of the OTU protease (2.72 Å), indicating a potential contact inhibitor to suppress OTU protease. Pep42 demonstrated the most extensive hydrogen bonding network, mediating five hydrogen bonds with key residues Asp88, Arg92, Trp99, and Ser101 of the OTU protease, with bond distances ranging from 1.82 to 3.33 Å (Table 6). These interactions suggest Pep42 might occupy a binding site similar to that of UbV, potentially mimicking critical contacts necessary for enzymatic inhibition. Collectively, these findings suggest that the shortlisted peptides engaged crucial residues within the OTU protease active site, potentially mimicking the inhibitory binding mode of the ubiquitin variant. This indicates their promise as novel peptide inhibitors targeting the deubiquitinase function of the CCHFV OTU protease, warranting further validation via MD simulation and in vivo studies.

The dynamical properties of these complexes were evaluated to relate structure to function, particularly in the context of OTU protease inhibition by peptides and compared with UbV. The preliminary analysis based on RMSD demonstrated consistent stability of all systems. Among all complexes, OTU protease-Pep42 complex exhibited a slightly more conformational variation. RMSF analysis was used to evaluate the dynamic flexibility of the protein when bound to peptides, including UbV, by assessing residue-level fluctuations. The binding of Pep23 and Pep42 was responsible for the enhanced dynamic flexibility of the protein, with Pep23 affecting the flexibility of both catalytic sites of OTU protease (Kocabaş and Ergin 2016). The flexibility pattern of each amino acid residue of the OTU proteases was found to be consistent in both OTU protease bounds with UbV and Pep31. Besides them, OTU protease becomes more dynamic due to Pep31, as depicted in Fig. 4c. UbV and peptides affect the flexibility of the OTU proteases, which suggests the potential for structural or conformational modifications.

sec.title: Dynamics and conformational effects
sec.p: Since the peptides’ functions depend on their unique conformational behavior. the observed structural variations and flexibility patterns in complexes with Pep23 and Pep42 suggest that their inhibitory potential arises from induced conformational changes in the OTU protease, particularly around the catalytic sites. The change in the secondary structure elements was evaluated for UbV, peptides, and OTU protease in the complexes. Pep23 and Pep42 affecting the protein structure were responsible for the variation in the protein’s secondary structure elements shown in Fig. 4d. The presence of polar, disorder-promoting residues in Pep23 and Pep42 known to destabilize secondary structures of peptides42 (Fig. 4e). In all complexes, UbV bound to the OTU protease exhibited a stable secondary structure throughout simulation time as seen in Fig. 4e, indicating that the UbV maintains its structural integrity upon binding and likely contributes to stable complex formation with the OTU protease. The structural variations in peptides suggested that their dynamic flexibility helped accommodate them at the binding site of OTU protease. Pep23 also perturbed the secondary structure of the protein’s catalytic site-2 of OTU protease. The comparative analysis of biochemical properties of the peptides demonstrated Pep31 having a high fraction of hydrophobic residues, whereas Pep23 and Pep42 comprise highly polar and disorder-promoting residues. The predominant hydrophobic residues in Pep31 facilitated stronger protein-peptide interactions due to hydrophobic and van der Waals (vdW) forces43, demonstrating its distinct binding compared to other peptides, as also deduced from their distinct interaction profiles. The PPIs between OTU protease and peptides including UbV revealed different binding patterns in these complexes which reflected the effect of different biochemical compositions of peptides on their binding modes. The high fraction of H-bonds in OTU protease-UbV and OTU protease-Pep23 complexes suggested that electrostatic interactions play a critical role in stabilizing these complexes. In contrast, the high content of hydrophobic residues in Pep31 favors van der Waals (vdW) interactions, creating a predominantly hydrophobic binding interface. This preference for hydrophobic contacts explains the lower number of residues involved in electrostatic interactions, which is consistent with the peptide’s amino acid composition (Fig. 5c). Strong vdW contacts between Pep31 (residues B.S185 and B.S186) and the catalytic residue, A.C40 and a π-cation interaction involving B.F189, highlighted alternative stabilizing forces that can compensate for reduced H-bonding. The consistency between OTU protease-UbV interaction data and experimental findings reported previously, validated the accuracy of our docking and interaction analyses. The role of the protein’s residues, Q149, W241, I131, and R92 further confirmed the functional relevance of these interactions. Overall, these findings suggested that the peptides utilize distinct mechanisms to interact with OTU protease, leveraging either electrostatic or hydrophobic forces. Understanding these differences may guide the design of more potent peptide inhibitors by targeting specific interaction types and catalytic site residues.

sec.title: Binding energetics
sec.p: Binding affinity analysis provided valuable insights into the interactions between the peptides and the OTU protease. While UbV demonstrated the most favorable binding energy, its interaction profile was primarily driven by strong electrostatic and van der Waals forces, compensated by a high desolvation penalty, suggesting a stable OTU protease-UbV complex; however, its solubility or structural desolvation requirements may limit its efficiency under physiological conditions. Among all peptides, Pep31 emerged as a promising candidate against OTU protease, demonstrating a relatively balanced energy profile characterized by favorable electrostatic and van der Waals interactions with a moderate solvation penalty. This balance implied that Pep31 can maintain strong binding without incurring excessive desolvation costs, which is a desirable trait in therapeutic peptide design. The favorable contribution by hydrophobic and cysteine residues for Pep31 binding likely contributed to its stable interaction with the protease, emphasizing the role of specific residue types in optimizing binding affinity. In contrast, Pep23 and Pep42 yielded less favorable binding energies, driven by highly unfavorable electrostatic contributions despite favorable solvation energies. This pattern suggested a preference for the unbound (solvated) state, likely due to the dominance of polar or disordered residues, such as serine (S), threonine (T), and glutamine (Q), which may lead to destabilizing interactions or charge repulsion within the binding pocket (Lazaridis 2000). Strikingly, the per-residue energy decomposition analysis also highlighted that UbV achieved strong overall binding energy; however, it relied heavily on only a few key interactions. In comparison, Pep31 formed multiple favorable contacts with OTU protease residues, suggesting a more distributed and potentially more robust binding interface. Moreover, the fluctuating energetic contributions of a few residues in Pep42 case across simulation ensembles contributed to unstable interaction, thus further reducing its binding potential. These findings suggest that optimization of peptide inhibitors should consider not only maximizing favorable energy terms but also ensuring residue-level interaction stability and balancing gas-phase with solvation energies44. Overall, this study highlights the importance of considering both total binding energies and per-residue interaction profiles when evaluating peptide inhibitors. The good performance of Pep31, in terms of balanced energetics and stable binding interface, suggested it as a promising lead for further development against OTU protease.

sec.title: UbV and peptides modulate OTU dynamics
sec.p: To further explored the mechanism of peptide-mediated inhibition, essential dynamics were analyzed using PCA in combination with FEL calculations. These approaches provide insight into large scale collective motions and conformational states. The eigenvalue distribution indicated that the dominant motions are captured within the first few PCs. The OTU protease-UbV complex exhibited the highest contribution along PC1, reflecting coordinated collective motion, whereas OTU protease-Pep31 indicated relatively lower eigenvalues, suggesting restricted dynamics and enhanced stability. Projection of the initial two PCs (PC1 and PC2), shown different conformational behaviors. OTU protease-UbV and OTU protease-Pep31 demonstrated limited conformational dispersion and supporting the role of Pep31 as a dynamic mimic of UbV. In contrast, OTU protease-Pep23 and OTU protease-Pep42 exhibited broader distributions of eigenvectors, reflecting increased flexibility and sampling of multiple conformational substates. This result is consistent with RMSF and secondary structure analyses.

The above findings, further confirmed by performing FEL analysis. OTU protease-UbV and OTU protease-Pep31 showed sharp and well defined energy minima, indicating stable conformational states. In contrast, OTU protease-Pep23 exhibited a broader energy basin. While OTU protease-Pep42 displayed multiple distinct energy minima, suggesting significant conformational heterogeneity. Structural comparison of representative states confirmed minimal deviations in OTU protease-UbV and OTU protease-Pep31, whereas Pep23 and Pep42 induced noticeable conformational changes, particularly in flexible regions.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: Computational tools assume complete protease cleavage, whereas actual cleavage depends on sequence context and kinetics, leading to possible inaccuracies in predicted peptides. In addition, post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation or glycosylation are not considered, despite their significant effects on peptide structure and function. The approach also lacks membrane and serum context, although MD analysis has shown peptide stability, but degradation and transport in biological systems are still unknown. Immunogenicity and hemolytic activity are anticipated for shortlisted peptides; however, peptide delivery and stability present significant challenges. Consequently, these computational results should be regarded as a preliminary step towards the creation of more stable and clinically pertinent peptidomimetics, necessitating additional experimental validation.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In this study, we employed a comprehensive structure-based drug design approach combined with molecular dynamics simulations to identify peptide inhibitors targeting the OTU protease domain of the RdRP of CCHFV. Using peptides derived from Moringa oleifera, we computationally screened candidates that mimic the binding interface of endogenous ubiquitin and possess features of OTU protease inhibitor. Molecular docking and free energy calculations via MM/GBSA revealed three peptides, Pep23, Pep31, and Pep42, as favorable binders. During MD simulations, Pep23 and Pep42 affect the flexibility and secondary structure of the OTU domain, which may hinder the normal ubiquitin-OTU interaction. Both peptides showed less favorable binding profiles than others due to electrostatic repulsion and high solvation energy, indicating limited binding but favorable water solubility. However, Pep31 and UbV caused similar flexibility patterns. Among these two inhibitors, UbV demonstrated the most favorable binding energy, but its solubility or structural desolvation requirements may limit its efficiency under physiological conditions. In contrast, Pep31 emerged as a promising candidate, offering a balanced energy profile characterized by favorable electrostatic and van der Waals interactions with a moderate solvation penalty. Per-residue energy decomposition further highlighted Pep31’s ability to engage with the protease through a more distributed and consistent interaction pattern. Overall, this work provides critical molecular insights into OTU-targeted peptide inhibition and Pep31 as a promising lead compound for further in vitro examination followed by in vivo experimentation and ultimate preclinical development against incurable zoonotic CCHFV infection.
